parts.title: How Young Rats That Prefer or Avoid Alcohol, and Rats That Drink a Lot or a Little, Behave: It Depends on Their Family Line, Not on Whether They Are Male or Female
parts.abstract:
Most people first try alcohol during their teenage years. Drinking a lot at that age is linked to a higher chance of developing alcohol use disorder (AUD), a problem with drinking that causes harm, and/or substance use disorder (SUD), a problem with using other drugs. To study this, scientists breed rats over many generations so that some lines drink a lot of alcohol and others drink very little. These rats help us find the kinds of behavior that go along with a tendency to drink a lot or a little alcohol when they choose for themselves.

We used a behavior test called the multivariate concentric square field™ (MCSF). It is a large arena with several zones, built to feel more like a natural setting than a small box. A single test in the MCSF gives a full picture of how an animal behaves.

We wanted to describe the behavior of young rats from several family lines. Some lines were bred to drink a lot of alcohol (the P and HAD1/2 lines), and others to drink very little (the NP and LAD1/2 lines). We also included Wistar rats, which are ordinary lab rats that were not bred for any particular trait. The rats had never had alcohol. We tested each one once in the MCSF when it was between 30 and 35 days old.

We found no shared behavior pattern among the lines that drink a lot, and none among the lines that drink little. Being male or female made only a small difference. Within each pair of lines, the high-drinking and low-drinking rats behaved differently, but the HAD1 and LAD1 lines were very similar to each other.

The P rats were very active and showed more risk-taking behavior. The HAD2 rats were less active, spent more time looking for shelter, and avoided the open areas. The P rats' results match what doctors see in patients: a stronger family history of alcohol problems, together with risk-taking behavior, strongly predicts future alcohol use disorder, which often starts early in life. The HAD2 rats, on the other hand, behaved like people who tend to feel negative emotions. This kind of temperament is also linked to a greater risk of developing alcohol use disorder and/or substance use disorder, which often starts later in life.
parts.introduction_first:
Addiction is a complicated disorder. It is shaped by a person's surroundings, and by how those surroundings work together with their genes. Some personality traits also make a person more likely to become addicted, such as acting on impulse and seeking out new and exciting experiences. Addiction often comes together with other mental health problems, including anxiety and depression (Babor, 1992; Cloninger et al., 1996; Lesch and Walter, 1996; Merikangas et al., 1998; Kranzler and Rosenthal, 2003; Moss et al., 2007).

For alcohol use disorder (AUD), the genetic risk is around 50% (Verhulst et al., 2015; Reilly et al., 2017). This shows why having family members with AUD is an important risk factor (Reilly et al., 2017). To find out how much of the risk of developing AUD is passed down from parents to offspring, scientists have bred laboratory animals in two directions at once: some lines are bred to drink a lot of alcohol, and others to drink very little (Bell et al., 2012, 2016, 2017).
parts.introduction_rest:
Scientists around the world have bred rats in two directions at once, some lines to drink a lot of alcohol and others to drink very little. This has produced seven pairs of high- and low-drinking rat lines. In Chile, the University of Chile bred the bibulous (UChB) and abstainer (UChA) rats (Quintanilla et al., 2006). In Finland, the ALKO rats were bred as alcohol-drinking (AA) and non-alcohol-drinking (ANA) lines (Sommer et al., 2006). In Sardinia, the alcohol-preferring (sP) and non-preferring (sNP) rats were bred (Colombo et al., 2006). In Warsaw, the high-preferring (WHP) and low-preferring (WLP) rats were bred (Dyr and Kostowski, 2008). In Indiana, the P and NP rats were bred, and the HAD and LAD lines were bred twice, giving two copies, or replicates, of each (McBride et al., 2014).

The P/NP and HAD/LAD lines were bred using exactly the same rules for choosing which rats to breed from. The P/NP rats started from Wistar rats (Murphy et al., 2002), and the HAD/LAD replicates started from N/NIH rats, another common lab rat (Murphy et al., 2002). Because these lines were bred on purpose, scientists can now study the behavior (Roman et al., 2012), brain biology (Bell et al., 2012) and genes (McBride et al., 2012; Bell et al., 2017) that go along with breeding for high or low drinking. The high-drinking lines are also useful for testing new medicines that might treat alcohol use disorder (Bell et al., 2012, 2016, 2017).

Earlier studies mostly looked at adult males. More recently, a few more studies have looked at how behavior differs between males and females (Bell et al., 2014). Scientists have also only recently started to study what happens when young rats drink alcohol around the time they become teenagers. Both P and HAD rats drink more alcohol at that age, both when they drink steadily over time and when they drink in bursts, like a binge (Bell et al., 2014). Even so, we know little about how these lines behave as teenagers before they have ever had alcohol, especially the females. Studying this would help us understand how a family history of alcohol use disorder shapes behavior while a young animal is growing up (Bell et al., 2013, 2014).

The multivariate concentric square field™ (MCSF) is a behavior test built on ethoexperimental methods, which means it is based on how animals naturally behave in the wild. It is designed to give a full picture of how an animal explores, takes risks and looks for shelter (Meyerson et al., 2006). This lets us spot differences between individual animals, and differences caused by a treatment, in both teenagers and adults (for example, Palm et al., 2014; Karlsson and Roman, 2016; Wille-Bille et al., 2018; Lundberg et al., 2019; Gore-Langton et al., 2021).

The MCSF has already been used to compare adult males from different pairs of lines, and from within each pair (P/NP, the HAD/LAD replicates, sP/sNP and AA/ANA) (Roman et al., 2007, 2012; Roman and Colombo, 2009). The differences between the high- and low-drinking rats in a pair were not the same from one pair to another (Roman et al., 2007, 2012; Roman and Colombo, 2009). The high-drinking lines also differed a lot from one another (Roman et al., 2012). More recently, a changed version of the MCSF was used to look at differences after only a short time of breeding for drinking during the rats' teenage years. In that study, the high-drinking line spent more time looking for shelter and took fewer risks when tested as teenagers (Fernández et al., 2020). An earlier copy of the same breeding program, tested in a different test called the light-dark box, showed the same patterns (Fernández et al., 2017).

In this study, we wanted to use the MCSF to look more closely at how a genetic tendency to drink a lot or a little alcohol is linked to the behavior of teenagers before they ever meet alcohol. To do this, we tested male and female P/NP rats and HAD/LAD replicates 1 and 2 that had never had alcohol. We also included a group of Wistar rats, which are not bred for any particular trait, so we could compare the bred lines with ordinary lab rats. We had two goals. The first was to look at differences between the high- and low-drinking rats in each pair. The second was to look at differences among all the lines bred in the same way, that is, among all three high-drinking lines and among all three low-drinking lines. We expected to find differences between the high- and low-drinking rats in each pair that were similar to those seen in the adult rats (Roman et al., 2012). We also expected the HAD/LAD replicates to be similar to each other within each group, and to differ from the P/NP lines.
parts.methods:
## Materials and Methods

### The Rats, How We Kept Them, and Our Ethics Approval

We studied three kinds of rats. The first were the high-drinking lines: the P rats and the HAD1 and HAD2 rats. The second were the low-drinking lines: the NP rats and the LAD1 and LAD2 rats. The third were ordinary Wistar rats (strain RccHan:WI, from Envigo, Indianapolis, IN, United States). Table 1 gives the details. All the rats were delivered to our laboratory on the day they were weaned, which is when they stop drinking their mother's milk.

We kept the rats in pairs, always a male and a female of the same family line. Each pair lived in a plastic cage that we could not see through (22 × 44 × 20 cm), with sawdust on the floor. The rats could eat (7001 Teklad 4%, Envigo, Madison, WI, United States) and drink water whenever they wanted. The room was kept at 24 ± 1°C and about 50% humidity. The lights were on for 12 hours and off for 12 hours, but the cycle was reversed, so the lights went off at 10:00.

We told the rats apart by marking their tails with a marker pen, and we darkened the marks whenever they faded. Before we started any procedures, the rats spent 5 days getting used to their home cages. We did all the experiments during the dark part of the day. The committee that oversees animal care at the Indiana University School of Medicine approved our plan. It follows the NIH's Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (National Research Council, 2011).

**TABLE 1**

Details about the rats in the study. For each family line, the table shows how many rats we used of each sex, which generation they came from, how many litters they came from, how many pups were in each litter and of which sex, and how old they were when they arrived (in days after birth).

| Line | Number of rats per sex | Generation | Number of litters | Pups per litter and sex | Age when weaned or delivered (days after birth) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | 20 | S82–S83 | 11 | 1–3 | 22–25 |
| HAD1 | 19–20 | S70 | 8 | 2–3 | 23–25 |
| HAD2 | 20 | S69 | 9 | 1–4 | 22–25 |
| NP | 12 | S81–S82 | 6 | 2 | 23–27 |
| LAD1 | 12 | S70 | 6 | 1–4 | 24–26 |
| LAD2 | 12 | S69 | 11 | 2 | 22–25 |
| Wistar | 20 | n.a. | n.a. | n.a. | 22 |

n.a., not applicable; PND, postnatal day (days after birth).

### The Multivariate Concentric Square Field™ Test

The MCSF (Figure 1) has been described in detail before (Meyerson et al., 2006; Roman and Colombo, 2009). In short, the arena is 100 × 100 cm. It is divided into zones. In the middle is a large square (70 × 70 cm) with a circle in its center (the central circle, 25 cm across). Corridors surround the square on three sides. On the fourth side, a raised and lit "bridge" is divided into a slope, a bridge entrance, and the bridge itself. One corner has a dark room with a shelter (the dark corner room). Another corner has a raised hurdle with a floor full of holes.

The lighting in each zone was measured in lux, a unit of brightness. It was 15 lux in the central circle, 5–10 lux in the corridors and on the hurdle, and 500 lux in the middle of the bridge.

**FIGURE 1**

A drawing of the MCSF. Walls (solid black lines) or imagined boundaries (dashed lines) divide the arena into zones. BE, bridge entrance; CTRCI, central circle; DCR, dark corner room. Adapted with permission from Lundberg et al. (2019).

Before testing, we got the rats used to being handled for three days in a row. Each day, we handled each rat on its own, weighed it, and let it get used to a small travel cage. Between 30 and 35 days after birth, each rat was tested once in the MCSF.

On test days, we carried the rats in their home cages, with the lights off, to a holding room. There, we left them undisturbed for 2 hours before the test began. We then used the travel cage to carry each rat, one at a time, to the testing room, and back again when the test was over.

On each test day, we first let a rat that was not being tested explore the arena. This way, the first rat to be tested would not affect the others. Males were always tested before females, and the two rats in a cage were never tested one right after the other.

A trial began when we released the rat into the center of the arena, facing the wall that did not lead to a corridor. Each trial lasted 20 minutes. Between rats, we sprayed the arena with a 10% alcohol (ethanol) solution, wiped it down, and let it air dry. After testing, we returned all the rats to the animal room, where we weighed them.

An overhead video camera filmed every trial, and we scored the videos by hand using the software EthoVision XT 13 (Noldus, Inc., Wageningen, Netherlands). For each zone, we recorded how long the rat took to visit it for the first time (the latency, in seconds), how many times it visited (the frequency), and how long it spent there (the duration, in seconds). We also counted how many times the rat reared up, groomed itself, and stretched out to reach for something (stretched attend postures). After each trial, we counted how many times the rat urinated and how many droppings it left in the arena.

We added up the frequency and duration in the corridors to get a total corridor measure. We also recorded how long the rat took to leave the center after the trial started. For each zone, including the total corridor, we then worked out three more measures. The first was the time spent per visit (duration divided by frequency). The second was the percentage of all visits that went to that zone. The third was the percentage of all time spent in that zone.

We also measured the rat's total activity, which is the sum of all its visits. We counted how many zones it visited and how long it took to explore the whole arena. Finally, we noted how often each zone was not visited, or each behavior was not done, by any rat in a group. For the corridors, we used only the total corridor measures, except for how often something happened, which we looked at for each corridor separately. To see how activity changed over the course of a trial, we split the total activity and the rearing counts into four 5-minute periods.

### How We Analyzed the Data

We did our statistics with the program Statistica 13 (TIBCO Software Inc., Tulsa, OK, United States), unless we say otherwise. First, we used the Shapiro-Wilk test to check whether each set of measurements followed a normal distribution, the familiar bell-shaped curve. Body weights did follow this curve. So we compared them with a factorial ANOVA, a test that checks whether the average differs between groups when two factors are involved. Here the two factors were family line and sex, and each rat belonged to only one group for each. We followed this with Tukey HSD tests, which compare the groups pair by pair.

The behavior measures from the MCSF did not follow a bell-shaped curve. So we used non-parametric statistics, which do not assume that shape. For measurements that can take any value, we used the Kruskal-Wallis test, which compares groups by ranking the values from smallest to largest. We followed it with Mann-Whitney U-tests, which compare two groups at a time, with a small adjustment (a continuity correction). For how often each zone and each behavior happened, we used a chi-square test, which compares counts between groups.

To study how activity changed over time in the MCSF, we used the program R 3.6.1 (R Core Team, 2019) with the nparLD package (Noguchi et al., 2012). This test looked at family line and sex as factors that each rat belonged to only once, and at time as a factor that each rat went through again and again. We followed it with two kinds of pair-by-pair tests. Wilcoxon's matched pairs test compared the same rats at different times. The Mann-Whitney U-test with continuity corrections compared different groups.

We analyzed the MCSF measures in two ways: with males and females analyzed separately, and with both sexes combined. Every follow-up comparison checked three things: (1) differences within each pair of lines, (2) differences within each set of lines chosen for a particular reason, and (3) differences between the Wistar rats and each of the selectively bred lines. Because we made many comparisons, we used the Bonferroni correction, which makes the bar for calling a result statistically significant stricter. We report only one level of significance, p < 0.05. This means a result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance alone less than 5% of the time. We also calculated effect sizes, which show how big a difference is, as described before (Fritz et al., 2012).

To look at the MCSF measures as a whole, we also used two methods that handle many measurements at once. The first, principal component analysis (PCA), looks at how a set of measurements relate to each other. Here, the set was the MCSF measures. The second, partial least squares projections to latent structures discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), looks at how a set of measurements relates to a single grouping. Here, the grouping was family line. We ran the PCA separately for each pair of lines, to get an overview of how each high-drinking line related to its low-drinking partner. We ran the PLS-DA to look at the differences between all the lines.

We let the software build the models automatically (a setting called autofit). We left out a component, one of the summary patterns the model finds, if its eigenvalue was below 2.0 or if its Q2 value was strongly negative. The eigenvalue shows how much of the variation a component explains, and Q2 shows how well the model predicts new data. We did not include latencies, how often something happened, percentage duration, or percentage frequency in the models. We left out other measures when the software advised us to.
parts.results:
## Results

We left five animals out of the analyses. Four were left out because of technical problems during testing: two HAD1 females, one Wistar female and one NP male. The fifth was a LAD1 female that spent more than 70% of the test climbing on the walls of the arena, so we had very little information about how she used the different zones.

Supplementary Figure 1 shows each animal's body weight on the day of testing. Females weighed less than males in the P, NP and Wistar rats. In the HAD1, LAD1, HAD2 and LAD2 rats, we found no difference in weight between the sexes. Overall, the Wistar rats were the heaviest, followed by the P rats and then the NP rats. The HAD1, LAD1, HAD2 and LAD2 rats were lighter than the P, NP and Wistar rats, but we found no differences in body weight among these four lines.

We also looked at whether being male or female changed the results of the MCSF test. We found no such differences in the P, NP, HAD1, LAD1 or HAD2 rats. Among the LAD2 rats, females urinated fewer times in the arena than males. Among the Wistar rats, females visited the center less often, as a percentage of all their visits, than males did (Supplementary Table 1). Because the effect of sex was weak, we discuss the rest of the results with males and females combined. To be open about it, Supplementary Table 1 gives the numbers and statistical results for each sex, alongside the results with both sexes combined.

### Comparing the Lines in Pairs

Figure 2A shows how big the differences were within each pair of lines. Figure 3 shows how often the rats went into each zone, how long they stayed there in total, and how long they stayed on each visit. Figure 4 shows two activity measures: total activity (the number of visits to all zones added together) and rearing (standing up on the hind legs). Figure 4 gives the totals for the whole 20-minute test, and Supplementary Figures 2A–F show how these changed over time, in 5-minute blocks. The remaining results are in Supplementary Table 1.

FIGURE 2

Color charts (heatmaps) of how big the statistically significant differences were: (A) between the high-drinking and low-drinking rats in each pair of lines, (B) among the three high-drinking lines, (C) among the three low-drinking lines, and (D) for each bred line compared with the Wistar rats. Number of rats: P n = 40; NP n = 23; HAD1 n = 37; LAD1 n = 23; HAD2 n = 40; LAD2 n = 24; Wistar n = 39. BE, bridge entrance; CTRCI, central circle; corr, corridor; D, duration (s); DCR, dark corner room; D/F, duration per visit (s); F (#), frequency (number of visits); H1/HAD1, high alcohol-drinking line, replicate 1; H2/HAD2, high alcohol-drinking line, replicate 2; L, latency (s); L1/LAD1, low alcohol-drinking line, replicate 1; L2/LAD2, low alcohol-drinking line, replicate 2; n.s., not statistically significant; NP, alcohol non-preferring line; Occ, occurrence (for zones not visited, or behaviors not done, by all animals); P, alcohol preferring line; SAP, stretched attend posture; TOTACT, total activity (sum of all frequencies); totcorr, total corridor; Wi, Wistar.

FIGURE 3

Results of the MCSF test in the bred rats. For each zone: (A) frequency (number of visits), (B) duration (s) and (C) duration per visit (s) in P, NP, HAD1, LAD1, HAD2 and LAD2 rats; (D) frequency (number of visits), (E) duration (s) and (F) duration per visit (s) in the central circle (CTRCI) for all lines. Each box shows the median (middle value) with the upper and lower quartiles (the range covering the middle half of the animals). Number of rats: P n = 40; NP n = 23; HAD1 n = 37; LAD1 n = 23; HAD2 n = 40; LAD2 n = 24. Stars mark statistically significant differences (p < 0.0023): between high- and low-drinking rats within each pair; P rats compared with P rats; NP rats compared with NP rats; H1 rats compared with HAD1 rats. We used a follow-up test that compares two groups at a time (Mann-Whitney U-test with continuity correction). BE, bridge entrance; CTRCI, central circle; DCR, dark corner room; HAD1, high alcohol-drinking line, replicate 1; HAD2, high alcohol-drinking line, replicate 2; LAD1, low alcohol-drinking line, replicate 1; LAD2, low alcohol-drinking line, replicate 2; NP, alcohol non-preferring line; P, alcohol preferring line; totcorr, total corridor.

FIGURE 4

Activity in the MCSF: (A) total activity (sum of all frequencies) and (B) rearing, in the bred lines and the Wistar rats. Each box shows the median with the upper and lower quartiles. Number of rats: P n = 40; NP n = 23; HAD1 n = 37; LAD1 n = 23; HAD2 n = 40; LAD2 n = 24; Wistar n = 39. Stars mark statistically significant differences (p < 0.0023): between high- and low-drinking rats within each pair; P rats compared with P rats; NP rats compared with NP rats; H1 rats compared with HAD1 rats; L1 rats compared with LAD1 rats (Mann-Whitney U-test with continuity correction). HAD1, high alcohol-drinking line, replicate 1; HAD2, high alcohol-drinking line, replicate 2; LAD1, low alcohol-drinking line, replicate 1; LAD2, low alcohol-drinking line, replicate 2; NP, alcohol non-preferring line; P, alcohol preferring line.

#### P and NP Rats

To see the overall pattern, we used a method called principal component analysis (PCA). It takes many measurements at once and boils them down to a few main directions, called components, that capture most of the differences between animals. We then plotted each animal's score on these components. For the P and NP rats (63 animals, 4 components), the first two components captured 63% of the differences between animals (R2X = 0.63), and the analysis could predict 28% of the differences when checked on data left out of the analysis (Q2 = 0.28). The plot (Figure 5A) confirmed that sex had only a small effect. It also showed that the line influenced how the P and NP rats behaved in the MCSF.

The P rats' scores leaned more strongly toward the positive side of component 1 than the NP rats' scores did, although the two lines overlapped somewhat. Within each line, males and females did not separate. The loading plot (Supplementary Figure 3A) shows which measurements contributed most to each component. The P and NP rats separated mainly along the first component (Figure 5A). The P rats' behavior was linked to total activity, to visits to the zones (except the dark corner room), and to time spent at the bridge entrance and on the bridge. The NP rats' behavior was linked to time spent in the corridors, and to time per visit to the hurdle, the slope, the bridge entrance and the bridge (Supplementary Figure 3A).

FIGURE 5

Plots of each animal's scores from the PCA of the MCSF measurements: (A) P and NP rats [n = 63, 2 of 4 components shown, R2X(1–2) = 0.46, Q2(1–2) = 0.29]; (B) HAD1 and LAD1 rats [n = 60, 2 of 2 components shown, R2X(1–2) = 0.54, Q2(1–2) = 0.27]; and (C) HAD2 and LAD2 rats [n = 64, 2 of 3 components shown, R2X(1–2) = 0.46, Q2(1–2) = 0.24]. Colors show the line, and shapes show males (circles) and females (upside-down triangles). The matching loading plots are in Supplementary Figure 3. HAD1, high alcohol-drinking line, replicate 1; HAD2, high alcohol-drinking line, replicate 2; LAD1, low alcohol-drinking line, replicate 1; LAD2, low alcohol-drinking line, replicate 2; NP, alcohol non-preferring line; P, alcohol preferring line.

When we compared the lines directly, P rats visited the corridors, the hurdle, the slope, the bridge entrance and the bridge more often than NP rats (Figures 2A, 3A). This gave the P rats higher total activity (Figures 2A, 4A). P rats spent less time in the corridors and in the dark corner room, but more time at the bridge entrance and on the bridge, than NP rats (Figures 2A, 3B). On each visit, P rats spent less time in the center, the corridors, the dark corner room and on the bridge (Figures 2A, 3C).

We also looked at each zone as a percentage of the whole arena. P rats spent a smaller share of their time in the dark corner room, and a smaller share of their time and fewer visits in the corridors, than NP rats (Figure 2A and Supplementary Table 1). The opposite was true at the bridge: P rats spent a larger share of their time there, and made more visits, than NP rats (Figure 2A and Supplementary Table 1).

We also followed activity over time, using total activity (Supplementary Figure 2A) and the number of rearings (Supplementary Figure 2B). The pattern over time was similar for P and NP rats. P rats were more active than NP rats in the second and fourth 5-minute blocks, and about equally active in the first and third. In both lines, activity started low, rose sharply and peaked in the second 5-minute block. After that, P rats' activity fell to a middle level during the second half of the test. NP rats' activity fell only in the fourth block, where it was about the same as in the first 5 minutes (Supplementary Figure 2A).

For rearing (Supplementary Figure 2B), we found no differences between the lines. P rats reared more in the second block than in the first, but apart from this, rearing did not change over time within either line. In short, P rats showed more exploring and more risk-taking behavior in the MCSF, while NP rats showed more behavior aimed at finding shelter.

#### HAD1 and LAD1 Rats

For the HAD1 and LAD1 rats (60 animals, 2 components), the first two components captured 54% of the differences between animals (R2X = 0.54), and the analysis could predict 27% of them (Q2 = 0.27). The plot (Figure 5B) shows that the two lines overlapped a great deal. Most animals from both lines clustered together, which shows that most animals behaved in a similar way. A few animals stood out, with a large negative score on component 1. The loading plot (Supplementary Figure 3B) showed that these unusual animals spent more time per visit in the dark corner room, on the hurdle and on the slope. These animals also did not visit every zone in the arena (Supplementary Data 1).

When we compared the lines directly, we found only a small difference between them. HAD1 and LAD1 rats did not differ in how often they visited any zone, or in how long they stayed there (Figures 2A, 3A,B,D,E). Time per visit was also the same for both lines (Figures 2A, 3C,F), except in the dark corner room, where HAD1 rats stayed longer on each visit than LAD1 rats (Figures 2A, 3C). Total activity and rearing did not differ between HAD1 and LAD1 rats (Figures 4A,B). However, a smaller share of HAD1 rats pooped in the arena, so HAD1 rats left fewer droppings than LAD1 rats (Figure 2A and Supplementary Table 1).

HAD1 and LAD1 rats changed their activity (total activity and rearing) only a little over time in the MCSF (Supplementary Figures 2C,D). LAD1 rats showed no changes over time. HAD1 rats were more active in the second 5-minute block than in the fourth (Supplementary Figure 2C). HAD1 rats reared more in the second block than LAD1 rats did (Supplementary Figure 2D), and also reared more in the second block than in the first and fourth blocks (Supplementary Figure 2D). In short, HAD1 and LAD1 rats behaved very similarly in the MCSF.

#### HAD2 and LAD2 Rats

For the HAD2 and LAD2 rats (64 animals, 3 components), the first two components captured 56% of the differences between animals (R2X = 0.56), and the analysis could predict 20% of them (Q2 = 0.20). The plot (Figure 5C) confirmed a small effect of sex and showed that the line influenced behavior in the MCSF. HAD2 rats' scores were spread widely across all four quarters of the plot, while LAD2 rats' scores clustered mostly in the lower right quarter (Figure 5C). This shows that the LAD2 rats varied less from one another. Within each line, males and females did not separate. The loading plot (Supplementary Figure 3C) shows which measurements contributed most. LAD2 rats stood out for their total activity, rearing, time in the corridors, and visits to the center, the central circle, the corridors, the dark corner room and the hurdle.

When we compared the lines directly, most of the differences between HAD2 and LAD2 rats involved the center and the central circle (Figure 2A and Supplementary Table 1). Compared with LAD2 rats, HAD2 rats visited the center and the central circle less often, both in number of visits (Figures 3A,D) and as a percentage of all visits (Figure 2A and Supplementary Table 1). They also spent less time in the central circle, both in seconds (Figure 3E) and as a percentage of their time (Figure 2A and Supplementary Table 1). On each visit to the center, HAD2 rats stayed longer (Figures 2A, 3C). Fewer HAD2 rats than LAD2 rats visited the central circle (Figure 2A and Supplementary Table 1).

Among the other measurements, HAD2 rats spent longer on each visit in the corridors and at the bridge entrance than LAD2 rats (Figures 2A, 3C). HAD2 rats reared less (Figure 4B). A smaller share of HAD2 rats visited corridor "b" and all the zones than LAD2 rats did (Figure 2A and Supplementary Table 1). HAD2 rats, on the other hand, visited the slope more often, as a percentage of all visits, than LAD2 rats, and groomed more often and in more bouts (Figure 2A and Supplementary Table 1).

The two lines did not differ in total activity in any of the 5-minute blocks (Supplementary Figure 2E). HAD2 rats became more active from the first block to the second and third, and were also more active in the second block than in the fourth. LAD2 rats became more active from the first to the second block, and showed no other changes over time. For rearing (Supplementary Figure 2F), HAD2 rats reared fewer times than LAD2 rats in the first, second and fourth blocks. LAD2 rats reared about the same number of times throughout, while HAD2 rats reared more in the second and third blocks than in the first. In short, HAD2 rats were less active than LAD2 rats in the MCSF and avoided the open areas more.

#### Comparing the High-Drinking Lines

Figure 2B shows how big the differences were among the high-drinking lines. Figure 3 shows how often the rats visited each zone, how long they stayed in total, and how long they stayed on each visit. Figure 4 shows total activity and rearing for the whole 20-minute test, and Supplementary Figures 2A–F show how these changed over time in 5-minute blocks. The remaining results are in Supplementary Table 1.

The P rats differed a great deal from both HAD lines. P rats visited every zone more often than either HAD line (Figures 2B, 3A,D), which gave them higher total activity than either line (Figures 2B, 4A). P rats also reared more than either HAD line (Figures 2B, 4B). On each visit, P rats spent less time in every zone than either HAD line (Figures 2B, 3C), with two exceptions. In the central circle, time per visit was the same for all lines (Figures 2B, 3F). At the bridge entrance, P rats spent less time per visit than HAD2 rats, but not than HAD1 rats (Figures 2B, 3C).

P rats spent more time in the center and the central circle than either HAD line. Compared with HAD2 rats, they spent more time on the hurdle and less time on the slope (Figures 2B, 3B,E). A larger share of P rats visited the whole arena than either HAD line. A larger share of P rats than HAD2 rats visited the central circle, the dark corner room and two of the corridors, and a larger share of P rats than HAD1 rats visited the slope (Figure 2B and Supplementary Table 1). Finally, compared with HAD2 rats, P rats left the center sooner at the start of the test, fully explored the whole arena sooner, and first entered the hurdle and the slope sooner. None of these timing measures differed between P and HAD1 rats (Figure 2B and Supplementary Table 1).

The two HAD lines also differed in some ways. HAD1 rats were more active in total than HAD2 rats (Figures 2B, 4A), because they visited the corridors and the central circle more often (Figures 2B, 3A,D). HAD1 rats also reared more than HAD2 rats (Figures 2B, 4B). HAD1 rats spent less time on the slope (Figures 2B, 3B) and less time per visit in every zone except the dark corner room, the hurdle and the central circle (Figures 2B, 3C,F) than HAD2 rats. HAD1 rats also left the center sooner at the start of the test, and first entered the hurdle, the bridge entrance and the bridge sooner, than HAD2 rats (Figure 2B and Supplementary Table 1). A larger share of HAD1 rats visited the whole arena and corridor "b", while a smaller share visited the slope and the bridge entrance, than HAD2 rats (Figure 2B and Supplementary Table 1).

Total activity in each 5-minute block (Supplementary Figures 2A,C,E) was higher in P rats than in either HAD line throughout the test. HAD1 and HAD2 rats were similar to each other, except in the first 5 minutes, when HAD1 rats were more active. P and HAD2 rats followed a similar pattern over time, although P rats' visit counts were about twice as high as HAD2 rats'. Both showed a clear rise to a peak in total activity in the second 5-minute block (Supplementary Figures 2A,E). HAD1 rats, by contrast, had a much flatter curve.

Rearing was also higher in P rats than in either HAD line, except in the second block, when P and HAD1 rats did not differ. HAD1 rats reared more often than HAD2 rats throughout the test. For rearing, the lines followed a more similar pattern over time, with all three lines rearing more in the second block than in the first.

We also used a second method, called partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA). It looks for the combination of measurements that best tells the groups apart, here the lines. We used it on all 187 rats, with 3 components. The first two components captured 57% of the differences between animals (R2X = 0.57) and 26% of the differences between lines (R2Y = 0.26), and the analysis could predict 22% of the differences between lines (Q2 = 0.22). The plot (Figure 6) shows that the three high-drinking lines differed mainly along the first component (Figure 6A). P rats' scores leaned toward the negative side of component 1. HAD1 rats' scores clustered around the center of the plot. HAD2 rats' scores leaned mostly toward the positive side of component 1 and sat mostly in the lower right quarter (Figure 6A). HAD1 rats had a group of unusual animals in the upper right quarter (Figure 6A), which was also a group of unusual animals in the PCA plot (Figure 5B).

The loading plot (Figure 6B) shows how the lines and the MCSF measurements were linked. For each line, we made a single combined measure that stands for that line. The P rats' combined measure leaned toward the negative side of component 1 and a little toward component 2. This was linked to visits to all zones, total activity, time in the central circle and the number of rearings. The HAD1 rats' combined measure sat in the upper right quarter, leaning more toward component 2 than component 1. This was linked to grooming, and to time and time per visit on the hurdle and in the dark corner room. The HAD2 rats' combined measure sat in the lower right quarter, leaning about equally toward components 1 and 2. This was linked to time on the slope, the number of urinations and droppings, and time per visit in the center, on the slope and at the bridge (Figure 6B).

In short, the P and HAD lines did not share a common behavior pattern. P rats were very active in the arena and showed more risk-taking behavior, while HAD2 rats were less active and showed more risk-avoidance and shelter-seeking behavior. The HAD1 rats fell in between the other two high-drinking lines.

Colors show the line, and shapes show males (circles) and females (upside-down triangles). #### Comparing the Low-Drinking Lines

Figure 2C shows how big the differences were among the low-drinking lines. Figure 3 shows how often the rats visited each zone, how long they stayed in total, and how long they stayed on each visit. Figure 4 shows total activity and rearing for the whole 20-minute test, and Supplementary Figures 2A–F show how these changed over time in 5-minute blocks. The remaining results are in Supplementary Table 1.

The NP rats differed a great deal from both LAD lines. NP rats visited the center, the corridors, the dark corner room, the hurdle and the central circle more often than either LAD line, and visited the slope more often than LAD2 rats (Figures 2C, 3A,D). This gave NP rats higher total activity than either LAD line (Figures 2C, 4A). NP rats also reared more than either LAD line (Figures 2C, 4B).

On each visit, NP rats spent less time in the center and the corridors than either LAD line. They also spent less time per visit at the bridge entrance than LAD1 rats, and less time per visit on the slope and on the bridge than LAD2 rats (Figures 2C, 3C). NP rats spent longer in the dark corner room than LAD1 rats, and less time on the bridge but more time in the corridors and the central circle than LAD2 rats (Figures 2C, 3B,E). NP rats took longer than LAD1 rats to first enter the bridge entrance and the bridge (Figure 2C and Supplementary Table 1). Finally, NP rats groomed less than LAD1 rats. Compared with LAD2 rats, they urinated fewer times, left fewer droppings, and had a smaller share of animals that pooped (Figure 2C and Supplementary Table 1).

The two LAD lines were mostly alike. LAD1 and LAD2 rats did not differ in how often they visited any zone, or in how long they stayed there (Figures 2C, 3A,B), and did not differ in total activity or rearing (Figures 2C, 4). However, LAD1 rats groomed more than LAD2 rats, reached the bridge entrance and the bridge sooner (Figure 2C and Supplementary Table 1), and spent less time per visit on the slope and on the bridge (Figures 2C, 3C).

When we split total activity and rearing into 5-minute blocks (Supplementary Figure 2), NP rats scored higher than either LAD line at every point in time, with a few exceptions. NP and LAD1 rats did not differ in total activity during the first 5 minutes (Supplementary Figures 2A,C), and none of the low-drinking lines differed in rearing during the last 5 minutes (Supplementary Figures 2B,F). For rearing, the low-drinking lines followed a similar pattern over time, with all three lines rearing about the same throughout. This is unlike the high-drinking lines (Supplementary Figures 2B,D,F). For total activity, by contrast, the lines within each pair matched each other more than the low-drinking lines matched one another (Supplementary Figures 2A,C,D).

In the PLS-DA (187 animals, 3 components; R2X = 0.57, R2Y = 0.26, Q2 = 0.22; Figure 6), NP rats' scores (Figure 6A) leaned a little to a moderate amount toward the negative side of component 1 and a little toward component 2. LAD1 rats' scores sat around the center of the plot, with a few unusual animals in the upper right quarter, while LAD2 rats' scores sat mostly in the lower right quarter. The loading plot (Figure 6B) shows that the combined measures for the low-drinking lines sat closer to the center than those for the high-drinking lines, but pointed in a similar direction. This shows that the low-drinking lines varied less from one another than the high-drinking lines did.

The NP rats' combined measure leaned toward the negative side of component 1 and very little toward component 2. This was linked to time spent in the corridors, and, to a lesser extent, to visits to each zone. The LAD1 rats' combined measure sat in the upper right quarter, close to the center. This was linked to time per visit in the dark corner room, and to time in the dark corner room and at the bridge entrance. The LAD2 rats' combined measure sat in the lower right quarter. This was linked to time spent in the center and on the bridge, and to time per visit in the center and in the central circle.

In short, the NP and LAD lines did not share a common behavior pattern, although they differed less than the high-drinking lines did. The two LAD lines were very similar to each other, while NP rats were more active and explored more in the MCSF than either LAD line.

#### Comparing the Bred Lines with the Wistar Rats

Figure 2D shows how big the differences were compared with the Wistar rats. Figure 7 shows how often the rats visited each zone, how long they stayed in total, and how long they stayed on each visit. Figure 4 shows total activity and rearing for the whole 20-minute test, and Supplementary Figures 2G,H show how these changed over time in 5-minute blocks. The remaining results are in Supplementary Table 1.

Each box shows the median with the upper and lower quartile. Stars mark statistically significant differences (p < 0.0023): Wistar rats compared with P rats; NP rats compared with NP rats; H1 rats compared with HAD1 rats; L1 rats compared with LAD1 rats; H2 rats compared with HAD2 rats; L2 rats compared with LAD2 rats (Mann-Whitney U-test with continuity correction). Wistar rats reared more during the test than either HAD or LAD line, but did not differ from the P or NP rats (Figures 2D, 4B). They were also more active in total than either HAD or LAD line, but did not differ from the P or NP rats (Figures 2D, 4A). This fits with the differences we saw in how often the rats visited each zone (Figures 2D, 3A,D, 7A,D). Wistar rats visited more often than HAD1 rats in 7 of the 8 zones, than HAD2 rats in all zones, than LAD1 rats in 5 zones, and than LAD2 rats in 6 zones. Compared with NP rats, they visited the bridge entrance and the bridge more often, and the corridors and the hurdle less often.

The same pattern held for time per visit (Figures 2D, 3C,F, 7C,F). Wistar rats spent less time per visit in most zones than the HAD and LAD lines, but differed less from the P and NP rats. Differences in how long the rats stayed in each zone were few overall (Figures 2D, 3B,E, 7B,E). The most noticeable were that Wistar rats spent more time in the central circle than either HAD or LAD line, more time in the corridors than P, HAD2 or LAD2 rats, less time in the dark corner room than P or NP rats, and less time on the slope than HAD2 or LAD2 rats.

Overall, Wistar rats were the quickest to leave the center and start exploring the rest of the arena, and they reached many zones quickly. However, the time they took to fully explore the arena differed only from HAD2 and LAD2 rats. Wistar rats also differed in how often they visited only two zones, and only compared with HAD2 rats (Figure 2D and Supplementary Table 1).

When we followed total activity over time (Supplementary Figures 2A,C,E,G), Wistar rats were more active than all the bred lines in the first 5 minutes. They stayed more active than either HAD or LAD line throughout the test, except compared with LAD1 rats in the third 5-minute block. From the second block onward, Wistar and NP rats were about equally active, while Wistar rats were less active than P rats during the last two blocks. Wistar rats' activity fell from the first half of the test to the second, a pattern that no other line showed.

For rearing over time (Supplementary Figures 2B,D,F,H), Wistar rats reared more than either HAD or LAD line throughout the test, except compared with HAD1 rats in the second 5-minute block. Wistar rats did not differ in rearing over time from P or NP rats. Wistar rats reared more in the first 5 minutes than in any later block. This pattern over time matched the high-drinking lines more closely, although no other line showed such a clear and lasting rise in rearing over the test.

In short, Wistar rats differed a great deal from either HAD or LAD line, especially in how much they explored and took risks in the central circle. They differed less from the P and NP lines, but the differences were still clear, especially in activity at the start of the test. A PLS-DA that included all the rat lines (Supplementary Figure 4) supported this overall pattern. Wistar rats differed from all the bred lines, but were more similar to the P and NP lines than to the HAD and LAD lines.

## Discussion

In this study, we used the MCSF test to describe the behavior of young male and female rats that had never had alcohol. The rats came from Indiana family lines that had been bred over many generations to drink a lot of alcohol or to prefer it. We call these the high-drinking lines (P and HAD1/2) and the low-drinking lines (NP and LAD1/2). Being male or female made only a small difference in behavior across the lines. Much bigger differences showed up within each pair of lines and between the high-drinking and low-drinking lines.

The P and NP lines, and the HAD2 and LAD2 lines, differed from each other within their pairs. The HAD1 and LAD1 lines, however, were very similar. No single behavior pattern was shared by all the high-drinking lines, and none was shared by all the low-drinking lines. The high-drinking lines differed a great deal, especially in how active they were. The P rats were the most active, and the HAD2 rats were the least active. The low-drinking lines were more alike than the high-drinking lines were. Even so, the NP line differed from both LAD lines, and the two LAD lines were similar to each other.

### How the P and NP Lines Behaved

Our results for young rats differed from earlier studies of adult P and NP rats. One earlier study used the MCSF to describe adult male rats from five pairs of lines bred in two directions at once, including the P and NP lines and the HAD and LAD lines. It found that P rats were less active than NP rats (Roman et al., 2012). In our study, by contrast, the P rats were the most active of all six lines.

Other studies have used a different test, called the open field test, to measure how much rats move around. In that test, adult male P rats (Badishtov et al., 1995; Nowak et al., 2000; McKinzie et al., 2002; Roman et al., 2012) and adult female P rats (McKinzie et al., 2002) moved around more than NP rats did. Studies of young P and NP rats have given mixed results. When the rats were 33 to 40 days old, P rats were more active than NP rats after being given a saltwater (saline) injection, whether they were male or female (Rodd et al., 2004). When they were 20 or 28 days old, however, P and NP rats showed no difference (McKinzie et al., 2002).

We also found that young P rats showed more risk-taking behavior. This differs from earlier work that described adult P rats as showing more anxiety-like behavior, meaning behavior that looks like worry or fear (Stewart et al., 1993; Hwang et al., 2004; Pandey et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2010). Other studies, though, found no such differences between adult P and NP rats (Badishtov et al., 1995; Viglinskaya et al., 1995; Roman et al., 2012).

The earlier MCSF study of adult lines is especially interesting. It found that P and NP rats differed in risk-taking behavior in opposite directions, depending on whether the researchers took into account how active the rats were overall. When they did not, male P rats took fewer risks than male NP rats. When they did, male P rats visited the risky areas more often, as a percentage of their visits, than male NP rats did (Roman et al., 2012). In our study, the results pointed the same way whether or not we took overall activity into account.

### How the HAD and LAD Lines Behaved

The differences we saw between the HAD and LAD lines also differed from earlier studies. Using various behavior tests, other researchers reported that adult male HAD and LAD rats were similar, both within each pair of lines and between the pairs (Viglinskaya et al., 1995; Overstreet et al., 1997; Hwang et al., 2004). Studies of young male and female rats found the same (Rodd et al., 2004). However, one study using the open field test and the elevated plus maze, a test in which rats walk along a raised cross-shaped path, found differences between the HAD and LAD lines (Roman et al., 2012).

In our study, the HAD2 rats stood out from the other HAD and LAD lines. They were less active and avoided the risky areas more. The HAD1, LAD1 and LAD2 lines followed the main pattern seen in other studies, which is that they are similar to each other. Notably, the HAD2 rats showed less risk-taking behavior in the CTRCI than the LAD2 rats did. The CTRCI is one of the measures from the MCSF test. Other researchers have seen this same difference before, between adult male HAD1 and LAD1 rats (Roman et al., 2012).

That earlier MCSF study of the adult lines found only small differences within each HAD and LAD pair, but larger differences between the pairs. HAD1 rats explored more than HAD2 rats, and LAD1 rats spent less time checking out the risky areas than LAD2 rats did (Roman et al., 2012). It is hard to say what our results mean for how young rats compare with adults. Earlier work has shown that, in young rats, the MCSF test does not separate general activity from exploring very well. It has also shown that young rats show less of the behavior of checking out risky areas than adults do (Lundberg et al., 2019).

An earlier study supports the idea that HAD1 and LAD1 rats are more alike than HAD2 and LAD2 rats, or P and NP rats. That study looked at how repeatedly taking alcohol away affected how much alcohol LAD1, LAD2 and NP rats drank (Bell et al., 2004). It found that LAD1 rats drank more alcohol after alcohol was taken away several times (Bell et al., 2004). This suggests that the gap between HAD1 and LAD1 rats may not be as large as the gap between HAD2 and LAD2 rats, or between P and NP rats.

### Differences Within the Lines Bred for the Same Trait

It is not entirely surprising that our results for young rats differ from earlier MCSF results for adults. One earlier study found that age affects behavior in the MCSF in male Wistar rats, which are ordinary lab rats (Lundberg et al., 2019). Our study shows a similar pattern for P and NP rats in the MCSF. Unexpectedly, this pattern is the reverse of what was found in adult male P and NP rats (Roman et al., 2012). The results for male HAD and LAD rats in that earlier study (Roman et al., 2012), however, were closer to ours.

Nowak et al. (2000) discussed why studies disagree about how P and NP rats, and to some extent HAD and LAD rats, behave. Some studies read their behavior as anxiety-like (Stewart et al., 1993; Hwang et al., 2004; Pandey et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2010). Others looked at how much they move around and how much they seek out new things (Badishtov et al., 1995; Nowak et al., 2000; McKinzie et al., 2002; Roman et al., 2012). Nowak et al. suggested that these findings may be linked to P and HAD rats reacting more strongly to new things. They also suggested that, in a new place where there is no way to escape, these rats are more likely to act as if they are trying to escape rather than exploring (Nowak et al., 2000).

Our findings do not support this idea. P rats showed more risk-taking behavior and were more active, which may be explained by seeking out new things and exploring more. Also, the HAD2 rats were not active and spent a lot of time looking for shelter, which goes against this idea (Nowak et al., 2000). So more research is needed to tell these different kinds of behavior apart.

The differences we found between the P and HAD lines may be explained by the fact that they came from different starting groups of rats. The P and NP lines were bred from Wistar rats, and the HAD and LAD lines were bred from N/NIH rats (Murphy et al., 2002; Bell et al., 2012, 2016). Our own results support this. When we compared the bred lines with Wistar rats, the P and NP rats were more like the Wistar rats than the HAD and LAD lines were. However, Wistar rats from different suppliers can differ a lot, for example in their behavior and in how much alcohol they choose to drink (Palm et al., 2011a,b, 2012; Goepfrich et al., 2013; Momeni et al., 2015; Wood et al., 2016).

The P and NP lines have been bred for more than 40 years (Lumeng et al., 1977). So we cannot be sure that the P and NP rats in our study were similar to Wistar rats because they share the same family history. Unfortunately, N/NIH rats are no longer sold, and only a few research groups keep them. This meant we could not include them as an extra comparison in this study.

Because the lines came from different starting groups, different genes for other behaviors are likely to have been passed down together with the genes for how much alcohol the rats drink and whether they like it. This is true for each pair of lines (for example, Tabakoff et al., 2009; McBride et al., 2012, 2013; Saba et al., 2015). Our finding that HAD1 and HAD2 rats differ, unlike earlier research, may be a recent change. It may have happened since the two lines in each pair were bred separately. Or it may be a difference in young rats' behavior that has been there all along the history of these lines but had not been noticed before.

An earlier study described the behavior of adult male rats that had never had alcohol in the MCSF. It included the Finnish AA and Sardinian sP lines, which were not part of our study. In that study, these two lines showed opposite extremes of behavior, while the P and HAD1/2 lines fell in between and were more alike (Roman et al., 2012). In our study, the P and HAD1/2 lines seemed to behave less alike when young than when they were adults.

Interestingly, another study bred rats for only a short time, based on how much alcohol they drank when young, and also found a clear difference in how the lines behaved when young (Fernández et al., 2020). In that study, the high-drinking line seemed most like the HAD2 line in our study. This shows why it is important to study the behavior of young rats from several high-drinking lines before they have ever had alcohol. That way, we can see the full range of behaviors that go along with these lines, which represent the different kinds of alcohol use disorder that these lines model.
